doc.title: Butch Miles interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Playing behind the beat and Bobby Plater's advice
summary: The Basie ensembles played behind the beat; Bobby Plater told him to lock in with the rhythm section, and no other band could do it.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Yeah, if he wasn’t playing, you sure missed it, but it added so much to the band and to the Basie sound. There were a lot of amazing things about the Basie sound that were very difficult. No other band has ever sounded quite like that. It’s like no other band ever really sounded like Duke’s band either. There were a lot of things where maybe the entire reed section in ensemble would play behind the beat. All five of them would play behind the beat and when we’d come back they’d come in together. Or the brass might have a quarter note triplet and on one particular arrangement it would be perfectly in time and on another arrangement they’d lay back on it. Or things like that. Or they’d clip a note, where sometimes you might figure a horn player would play the full value, they might clip it because that was the way that they were interpreting. And Bobby Plater came up to me one time we were playing — oh darn — I think it was “Moten Swing” I’m trying to remember if that is the arrangement. Now see I’m getting these arrangements mixed up in my head. But there’s a sax ensemble in the middle of one of those charts which is just amazing, incredible. And they would start off smack on the beat and then by the time they were into the first or second bar they were behind, they were phrasing behind, but all five of them were phrasing together. And boy the first few months I was on the band I wasn’t used to that. You see I was always used to this, it had to be played this way. That was the way I thought, I had very, like tunnel vision, where tempos went. And Bobby finally came to me one day and says, “listen, when we get to that section, don’t listen to us. Lock in to the rhythm section, and get that section strong, and let us do what we’re going to do ‘cause we’re going to rely on you. If you start listening to us the whole thing is going to start to go like this like woah.” He said, “you can’t do that. We’ll come back
in right, we’ll get out just in time.” But this was a Basie trademark, and I had to take that advice and burn it into my memory. He was absolutely correct.
Did you find that other bands either didn’t have that flexibility or were afraid to let sections of the band fall back like that?
